name: Dorsal raphe nucleus
summary: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the largest serotonergic nucleus of the brain, a midline column in the ventral periaqueductal gray of the caudal midbrain and rostral pons, beneath the aqueduct and between the trochlear nuclei and the medial longitudinal fasciculi. Its neurons send serotonin to the cortex, striatum, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus and regulate mood, anxiety, impulsivity, appetite, sleep and pain, forming the anatomical target of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. It fires during waking and falls silent in REM sleep, it inhibits the trigeminovascular system in migraine, and it degenerates early in Parkinson disease, contributing to the depression and sleep disturbance that precede the motor signs.

anatomy.location: Ventral part of the periaqueductal gray in the midline of the caudal midbrain and upper pons, extending from the level of the oculomotor nucleus to the locus coeruleus, between the two medial longitudinal fasciculi and above the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles.

afferents.via: medial forebrain bundle and local fibers

efferents.to: Cerebral cortex, striatum, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus
Substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area
Spinal trigeminal nucleus and dorsal horn

function: Dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons project rostrally through the medial forebrain bundle to the whole forebrain, where serotonin acting through many receptor subtypes modulates cortical excitability, the emotional responses of the amygdala, the reward computations of the striatum and the stress reactivity of the hippocampus; they promote patience and behavioral inhibition, suppress feeding and pain, and their tonic activity is high in waking and absent in REM sleep, permitting the REM-on neurons of the pons to fire. The nucleus receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral habenula, the hypothalamus and the locus coeruleus, and its neurons express autoreceptors whose desensitization underlies the delayed onset of antidepressant action. Descending projections modulate the trigeminal nucleus and dorsal horn.

midline caudal midbrain beneath the aqueduct

imaging.normalAppearance: The midline periaqueductal gray of the caudal midbrain on axial images at the level of the inferior colliculus; it is not distinguishable from the surrounding gray on clinical MRI.

pathology.finding: Reduced serotonin transporter binding in the raphe and its targets on PET, correlating with depression, fatigue and sleep disturbance; MRI normal.
Small lesion of the caudal midbrain periaqueductal gray with vertical gaze and pupillary signs and mood or sleep change.
Periaqueductal FLAIR hyperintensity involving the raphe region with ophthalmoplegia and altered consciousness.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the wake-active serotonergic tone that gates REM sleep
Loss of descending serotonergic modulation of the trigeminal and spinal dorsal horns

examination: Mood, anxiety and impulse control history
Sleep pattern and REM behavior disorder
Headache history, since the raphe modulates the trigeminovascular system
pearls: The dorsal raphe is where antidepressants act, and why they take weeks: the autoreceptors must desensitize
Serotonin is the neurotransmitter of patience; its loss makes waiting impossible
Depression before parkinsonism reflects raphe degeneration that precedes the substantia nigra

pitfalls: Serotonin syndrome from drug combinations is a raphe overdrive: clonus, hyperthermia and agitation, not a structural lesion
